title: Checkpoint: Coasts and Islands
objective: After this level you can explain how waves, rivers and volcanoes shape coasts and islands.
summary: Surtsey rose off Iceland in 1963. Waves have since cut away about half of it, carving cliffs in its cracked lava, while its hard palagonite core holds on.

cards.headline: A new island rose off Iceland in 1963. The waves have been eating it since.
cards.body: Its name is Surtsey. In one young island's life you can watch almost every force from this chapter at work.

cards.fact: Surtsey lost about half its area to the waves in 35 years.
cards.context: The eruption broke the surface in November 1963 and kept going until June 1967, leaving an island of about 2.7 km². By 2002 the waves had cut it to about 1.4 km². Like Hawaii's islands in Level 64, it was built by a volcano. Unlike the Island of Hawaii, it has had no fresh lava since.

cards.headline: The weak spots go first
cards.body: The waves went after Surtsey's weak spots first, just like the caves of Level 62. In the southwest, where the lava was badly cracked, they broke down a strip of land up to 650 m wide and cut sea cliffs up to 75 m high. Elsewhere, the lava shielded the loose volcanic ash behind it. Cracks first, solid rock last.

cards.headline: The core that stays
cards.body: Surtsey's heart is palagonite tuff, volcanic ash hardened into rock, and it stands up to the sea far better than loose ash or cracked lava. Researchers expect that after about 160 years only that core will be left, ringed by steep cliffs. Volcanoes build islands. Waves decide how long they last.

mascot.line: An island that's shrinking on schedule. Geologists get to watch the whole show.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: Sand: worn rock, shattered lava, shells and parrotfish
Waves quarry, grind and undercut, weak spots first
Hot spot islands sink; reefs make atolls
Surtsey: built by fire, trimmed by waves

questions.prompt: Coasts and Islands recap: about how much of Surtsey's area had the waves removed by 2002?

options.label: About a tenth
options.rationale: Much more: it went from about 2.7 to 1.4 km².

options.label: About a quarter
options.rationale: More: 2.7 km² down to 1.4 km² is about half.

options.label: All of it
options.rationale: Surtsey is still there, about 1.4 km².

questions.explanation: Surtsey shrank from about 2.7 km² in 1967 to about 1.4 km² by 2002: roughly half.

questions.prompt: Coasts and Islands recap: why is Surtsey's palagonite core expected to outlast the rest of the island?

options.label: It's still erupting and adding fresh rock
It's much tougher than loose ash or cracked lava
It sits in water too calm for big waves
options.rationale: Waves are eroding the whole coast; the core resists them.

options.label: A coral reef has grown up around it
options.rationale: Surtsey is in cold Icelandic water with no reef.

questions.explanation: Palagonite tuff is volcanic ash hardened into rock; it resists wave erosion far better than loose ash or cracked lava.

questions.prompt: Coasts and Islands recap, from Level 61: what color is the sand that forms when lava shatters as it meets the sea?

options.label: Pink
options.rationale: Pink sand comes from foram shells.

options.label: Pure white
options.rationale: White tropical sand is ground coral.

options.label: Tan
options.rationale: Tan sand is quartz and feldspar from rock inland.

questions.explanation: Lava cools and shatters as it enters the sea, making black sand, as on Hawaii's black beaches.

questions.prompt: Coasts and Islands recap, from Level 65: a volcanic island sinks while its fringing reef keeps growing upward. What does it become in the end?

options.label: A sea stack
options.rationale: Stacks are left when sea arches collapse.

options.label: A ria
options.rationale: A ria is a drowned river valley.

options.label: An estuary
options.rationale: An estuary is where a river meets the sea.

questions.explanation: When the island sinks out of sight, the reef remains as a ring around a lagoon: an atoll.

questions.prompt: Coasts and Islands recap, from Levels 61 and 69: what do rivers supply that keeps many beaches from wasting away?

options.label: Fresh water that hardens the sand
options.rationale: Beaches need new sand, not water.

options.label: Sand worn from rock farther inland
Salt that glues the grains together
options.rationale: Salt doesn't hold beaches in place.

options.label: Mangrove seeds that anchor the dunes
options.rationale: The supply that matters is sediment.

questions.explanation: Rivers carry worn-down rock to the coast as sand; coasts starved of that sediment erode and move inland.
